title: Same $7,500 in a taxable brokerage
audience: People who think maxing a Roth alone is enough and who also need to invest beyond the IRA limit
thesis: Put $7,500 a year in a Roth for 30 years and a brokerage gets you 60-70% of the same outcome. The Roth is the cornerstone — but not the whole portfolio.

concepts.label: The 30-year outcome gap
concepts.body: Same $7,500 a year for 30 years at 7% real return. The Roth IRA ends at roughly $708,000, all tax-free. The taxable brokerage ends at roughly $570,000 — but you keep every dollar. The gap is $138,000, not millions.
concepts.source: Future-value of an annuity, FV = PMT × [((1 + r)^n - 1) / r] with r=0.07; long-term capital gains rate 15%

concepts.label: Why the gap is smaller than you think
concepts.body: The taxable brokerage has two tax events the Roth doesn't: dividends taxed annually, and capital gains on sale. The long-term capital gains rate is 15% — much lower than ordinary income. With a low-turnover index fund, the drag is roughly 0.5% per year.
concepts.source: IRS Pub 550; long-term capital gains rates

concepts.label: When the brokerage wins
concepts.body: The brokerage wins on flexibility: no contribution limit, no income phaseout, no early-withdrawal penalty, no 5-year rule. Use it for amounts above the Roth limit, for early-retirement bridge income, or for money you might need before 59½.
concepts.source: IRC §1(h) capital gains rates; SECURE 2.0 RMD changes

sources: IRS Pub 550 — investment income and expenses
S&P 500 historical real return 7% (Damodaran data, NYU Stern)
